speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, I move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head R of the Estimates be reduced by $100." Chairman, I am a disputes lawyer in an international arbitration practice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has firmly established itself as a leading international dispute resolution hub, attracting parties from all over the world seeking a neutral, efficient and trusted venue for resolving their disputes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our strategic location, strong rule of law and world-class legal institutions make us the preferred choice for businesses and investors navigating complex cross-border disputes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: SIAC's caseload has grown steadily over the years, reflecting the confidence of the global business community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC) has seen an increase in cases involving international parties, reinforcing our reputation as a trusted forum for commercial dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Beyond arbitration and litigation, Singapore is also a leader in mediation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With a robust legal framework, top-tier professionals and a commitment to innovation, Singapore will continue to serve as a premier dispute resolution hub, offering certainty and fairness in an increasingly complex global business environment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has, over the years, succeeded in attracting inter-governmental dispute resolution institutions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Permanent Court of Arbitration has an office here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All around us, various jurisdictions have made significant developments and there is new competition for talent and disputes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just this year, the new Abu Dhabi International Arbitration Centre (Arbitrate AD) was launched with new arbitration rules that emphasise transparency, efficiency and cost effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A significant change is that the Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM), is now the default seat of arbitration, unless otherwise agreed, shifting from the previous onshore Abu Dhabi framework.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, in his Chinese New Year dinner, mentioned Singapore has to: first, stay open in this tumultuous economic climate to attract the right talent and investments to Singapore; second, stay ahead of the competition and ahead of the curve; but at the same time, third, stay united as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Now, in this spirit, may I ask the hon Minister what more is the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) doing to maintain our competitive edge on this front?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is MinLaw doing to support the legal profession to better meet the demands of modern legal practice to strengthen Singapore as a leading legal and dispute resolution hub?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Chairman, access to justice must be real and meaningful for the common person, ensuring that legal protections work for those who need them the most.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Singapore has taken concrete steps to make justice accessible, especially in key areas affecting everyday lives.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: For families and divorced mothers, enforcing maintenance orders is critical.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The Maintenance Enforcement Process (MEP) now helps ensure that spouses and children receive the financial support that they are legally entitled to, reducing delays and hardship.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In May 2023, the Family Justice Reform Bill was passed by Parliament and received Presidential assent.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The Family Justice Reform Act seeks to, among others: firstly, make improvements to Court proceedings and procedure in the Family Justice Courts; and secondly, enhance MEP.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: What is the status of the changes to be implemented through this Act?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The Protection from Harassment Act (POHA) provides Expedited Protection Orders against cyberbullying and harassment, ensuring that victims, including the vulnerable, can seek redress quickly.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In this regard, the Prime Minister has announced that a new agency will be set up to deal with online harms and that the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) and MinLaw are working together on this piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: What measures does MinLaw have in mind for addressing online harms?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: For those in financial distress, the personal bankruptcy regime has been reformed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: While over 1,600 bankruptcy orders were made in 2022, many benefited from the Debt Repayment Scheme, which offers a structured way to repay debts without the severe consequences of bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Bankruptcy applications have increased in recent years as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Does MinLaw consider that reforms to Singapore's bankruptcy law are necessary to address the evolving financial landscape?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Singapore remains committed to ensuring that legal protections truly serve those who need them the most.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, it has been barely three decades since the Internet was first introduced into most of our lives.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many of us in this House may remember life and childhoods without the Internet.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For the children of today, this is almost unthinkable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As Internet use has become a ubiquitous part of life, the potential for online harms has also grown.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The issue of scams, many of which take place online, has just been discussed in the Ministry of Home Affairs' (MHA's) Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Other types of online harms include exposure to harmful online content or conduct, including explicit or violent materials, cyberbullying and harassment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Addiction to screens is also a problem, especially with children and youths; and countries, such as Australia, have passed legislation to limit access to social media for children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: He mentioned that MinLaw and MDDI are working together on this project.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In conjunction with this, I also note that a public consultation was held by MinLaw and MDDI to get feedback from the public.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Does MinLaw have any updates on this initiative, the likely legislative framework and details on the plans for this new agency?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of us who are on social media have faced all sorts of cyberbullying at one point or another.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, the bully makes false allegations; sometimes, they deliberately use words intended to humiliate and hurt your feelings; the trolls frequently make insinuations about your character, they use mean and vicious words against you.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Frequently, the bully hides behind the cloak of anonymity.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is not acceptable, especially for those younger social media users.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Why should anyone using social media be subject to such bullying behaviour?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update as to the new legislation?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Make it illegal for any social media user to use a false account to register that account.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This means that if any user wishes to, say, bully others by making false allegations or using mean or harsh words, they must be held to account for the things they say.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I look forward to the day when social media users can be protected from such bullying behaviour.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has developed a framework to address and mitigate these online harms through various legislation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Ministry's plans to establish a dedicated agency, codify statutory torts and lift the veil of anonymity, will serve to enhance accountability and fortify our efforts in this regard.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the assistance be augmented to support vulnerable victims, for example, children as well as women?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The agency will also be empowered to disclose the identity information of perpetrators to victims under specified circumstances.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will this be implemented in practice, given that many online platforms only require an email address for registration?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What if the user of the account is overseas, for example?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How else can the agency work with community groups to educate the public on constructive and safe online behaviour?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have seen how some lower-income Singaporeans struggle with this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A simple parking violation that usually attracts an out-of-Court composition fine is not paid, eventually leading to a Court hearing that requires a bailor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Failure to find a bailor will lead to pre-trial custody, which often leads to job loss or disruption of education, plunging the whole family into a much more precarious situation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I had previously raised this issue during the Justice System Motion in November 2020.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are there indications from the law enforcement agencies that more eligible persons are being released on personal bond?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, for those charged in Court, are there similar indications from the Courts that more accused persons are now being released on personal bond?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I also ask MinLaw how this Court has and can better ensure the efficient and effective resolution of harassment complaints.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The problem is that they may win the case and get a judgment either from the Courts or the Employment Claims Tribunal but their happiness and relief are often short-lived.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This is because the employer may not be able or want to pay up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This would mean the aggrieved worker, often a layman, having to navigate and be subjected to the entire rigmarole to enforce the judgment and also incur monies to do so.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister provide an update on reforms to address challenges of non-compliance with Court orders?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, the last few years have seen significant changes to improve access to justice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Thanks to initiatives from MinLaw, the Law Society, community organisations and, of course, the many lawyers that contribute their time and money to pro bono work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: On the Ministry's part, it set up the Public Defender's Office, a major initiative that now provides criminal defence services for impecunious defendants.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The Law Society has set up an Institution of Public Character called Pro Bono SG and through this, provided legal aid for those who need assistance in civil matters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In the Admiralty division, for example, the Realm of Tranquility, a local charitable organisation, collaborated with Pro Bono SG to open a community legal clinic at their premises which brings legal aid to the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: These are commendable initiatives and I would like to know if the Ministry has any further plans to facilitate access to justice?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: An important aspect of justice is also the ability to enforce judgements easily.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I will be grateful for any updates on this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Does the Ministry have any views on this matter and is it planning any further actions in relation to the bankruptcy regime?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Ensuring that legal services are accessible and affordable to all citizens, not only foster trust in the judicial system, but also supports the country's commitment to justice and equality for everyone, regardless of their background or circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In this context, how is the Ministry addressing the barriers faced by vulnerable populations in accessing justice and what strategies are in place to ensure their voices are both heard and protected?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: What initiatives are being introduced to make legal information and resources more available online?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: How is technology being leveraged to streamline legal processes, reducing the time and costs associated with accessing justice?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Restorative justice and community mediation are effective at resolving conflicts and addressing harm within communities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike traditional punitive systems, restorative justice focuses on healing and reconsolidation by involving all stakeholders in the process, including victims, offenders and the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Mediation serves as a collaborative tool, facilitating open dialogue and mutual understanding to reach amicable resolutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Together, these practices not only help reduce recidivism but also strengthen community bonds, promoting a more supportive and cohesive environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In this context, what initiative is the Ministry implementing to promote community mediation and resolution and how is this addressing challenges, such as public awareness and acceptance, to encourage broader participation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In what ways is the Ministry ensuring that legal professionals receive adequate training in community mediation and restorative justice principles and what partnerships are being formed between the Ministry and community organisations to facilitate the successful implementation of mediation and restorative programmes?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, I spoke on community disputes at last year's COS.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As many of us in this House have experienced, managing and resolving disputes among neighbours, often living side by side, is one of the most challenging aspects of the work we do in the Community.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Oftentimes, in disputes involving noise or other disagreements, it is a contest of one neighbour gathering "evidence" against the other.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This can include recording each other's alleged noise or movements at odd hours or, in extreme cases, surreptitiously installing cameras directed at each other's homes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As one can expect, such behaviour is likely only to escalate and rapidly increase the temperature of the dispute, often damaging neighbourly relations beyond repair.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Having an objective arbiter, like CRU, could reduce the need for extreme measures taken by the residents themselves, with decisions and outcomes acceptable to affected parties.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The online Community Justice and Tribunals System brings convenience to those who can go online.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens to seniors who are less digitally-savvy, less literate or who may not be so familiar with the English language?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens if these seniors want to access the Small Claims Tribunal or Protection from Harassment Court or other services under the CJTS?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Does this mean the digitally disadvantaged may inevitably face an uneven playing field when it comes to accessing community justice with all these new digital platforms?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Digital justice must not become difficult justice for the non-information technology (IT) savvy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must avoid digital dropout where a case with merits is abandoned, because a senior found it too hard to access digital processes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Chairman, in Singapore, pursuing a creative career can be difficult due to the challenge of earning a stable living.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: However, it is vital that Singaporean artists, writers, filmmakers and other creatives can lead meaningful livelihoods and help support the growth of Singapore's artistic and cultural landscape.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: To that end, I have come across many creatives, such as film producers and photographers, who do not fully understand their rights, especially when it comes to the intellectual property (IP).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This is a crucial gap in knowledge that must be addressed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This becomes more urgent and important with the rise of generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI), which has led to the unauthorised use of copyrighted materials for profit-driven purposes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The recent open statement from Singapore's literary community to the National Library Board, signed by at least 88 local creatives, reflects growing concern over the lack of regard for copyrighted works and its potential impact on the vitality and viability of pursuing an artistic career.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Besides promoting education and awareness, the Government can also consider introducing regulations on AI models to better level the playing field between AI developers and creatives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: For example, the European Union's (EU's) AI Act compels Gen AI models to demonstrate compliance with the EU's copyright law and provide a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training their models.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Such obligations empower copyright-holders to exercise their rights by opting out of having their works used in text and data mining.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In this regard, it would be good to understand whether there are ground outreach efforts to creatives to promote understanding of their IP rights.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In addition, how are MinLaw and the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) tackling the copyright challenges posed by AI.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: IPOS and the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) Visual, Audio, Creative Content Professionals Association (Singapore) is partnering to raise IP awareness and proficiency among creators.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Likewise, for companies that adopt AI, how will MinLaw guide them to adhere to ethical and respectful use of IP?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: For instance, copyrighted works should not be used to train Gen AI applications without permission or compensation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: How will MinLaw balance between fostering innovation and protecting creators' IP?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Keith Chua, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, there are many avenues for our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to grow both locally and internationally.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: How can IPOS support SMEs in this area?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Has IPOS worked with trade associations and chambers (TACs) to better reach Singapore SMEs?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has established herself as one of the leading places for international arbitration.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Recent reports suggest that Singapore has become the leading arbitration hub.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There are many accompanying benefits ranging from professional to economic.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is also keen competition from other cities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: With the many global and technological changes more recently, including a more protective and uncertain world, how might this affect our efforts?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In-house counsels in Singapore form a significant and growing part of our legal fraternity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This presents a great opportunity for our Singapore in-house legal counsels to differentiate themselves in their skills as well as how they help businesses move confidently in Singapore and around the globe, while also helping to bring back crucial work to our private practice lawyers and others in related fields.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I therefore ask MinLaw to provide an update of their current support and longer-term plans to further uplift the career health and progression of in-house counsels in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In the legal fraternity and ecosystem, we have a group of para-legals, also known as paraprofessionals or legal executives in law firms and corporate entities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Many of them graduated from the law programmes offered by Temasek Polytechnic as well as other educational institutions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: They also hope to build and boost their professionalism, competencies and standards, continuing education and career progression opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I therefore ask how can MinLaw further help to uplift and enhance the career health and progression of para-legals and paraprofessionals.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Chairman, I continue to speak up for law students and young lawyers in this Chamber.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: The demands of the legal industry on our juniors are not easy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: To keep pace with the fast-evolving demands of the profession and to take care of our young lawyers while maintaining a strong pipeline, it is essential to ensure that our legal training frameworks remain robust and forward-looking.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: For smaller firms operating as niche practices, arrangements must be made to rotate trainees to a covering law practice for them to gain exposure to a secondary seat.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Does the Ministry have any indication as to the capacity of smaller firms to undertake the training of young lawyers and recruit future talent, given the necessity of rotating trainees out of their firm?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Are measures being considered to support these firms in navigating such demands?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: With our growing role as a leading international arbitration hub, a rising number of disputes from our civil law neighbours may be heard on our shores.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Is the Ministry considering furthering educational reforms to deepen and broaden civil law expertise among our law students and practitioners to ensure that we can remain at the forefront of international dispute resolution?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Becoming a signatory to these conventions could strengthen Singapore's position as a global wealth management and family office hub.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It could enhance legal certainty in cross-border disputes, simplify estate and succession planning for internationally connected families, and provide greater safeguards for vulnerable individuals who are based in Singapore but who have legal or financial interests across multiple jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I would appreciate insights from the Ministry on any ongoing considerations, potential challenges or timelines for Singapore to join these conventions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Chairman, as our urban living grows increasingly dense, well-planned community areas are essential in creating dynamic and sustainable neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: The Ministry has stated that it had identified opportunities to optimise state properties to better meet community needs and create greater social impact.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: What criteria is used to evaluate which state properties should be redeveloped?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: What are the specific community needs that are taken into consideration, given our diverse demographic?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Does the Ministry have plans to pilot community concepts that engage a broader spectrum of Singaporeans so as to create dynamic spaces that foster meaningful interactions?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Could the Ministry consider piloting co-living concepts in these properties, for example, or create more care and recreational spaces for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Are any of the properties currently in use by the successful tenants?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: In evaluating the interest generated in the programme thus far, can the Ministry advise whether the interest for state land is still leaning towards the more conventional method as there seems to be many more sites listed for tender under this method?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Would there be favourable consideration by SLA for proposals from non-profit groups and organisations, given the increase in interest for arts, culture and heritage?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Some community service organisations may find use of state properties as an option to better connect with the community.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: As an example, creative use of a property may enable it to be a welcoming touchpoint for persons to find out more about difficult topics, such as mental health or other conditions like anxiety or depression.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Use of appropriate sites may also appeal to the seniors, especially if the property has an interesting history.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Chairman, state land assets are crucial to Singapore's urban planning and economic development.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: How has SLA successfully optimised state assets to meet community and economic needs?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chairman, this year, we celebrate SG60 and our nation-building efforts that have allowed Singapore to develop, prosper and thrive against the odds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many factors have contributed to our transformation from Third World to First, and one of them is our commitment to building a strong legal system and advancing the rule of law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw will continue to uphold these fundamentals, to ensure the vibrancy of our economy, as well as to maintain trust and cohesion in our society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My colleague, Minister of State Murali Pillai, will speak about optimising the use of state assets and safeguarding our society from online harms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are undoubtedly strong headwinds and we have to be cautious.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But equally, in this environment, there are also opportunities if we remain attractive to foreign investments and maintain an open, thriving business environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One reason Singapore has been able to attract foreign investments is the confidence in our legal system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry is committed to preserving and enhancing this trust in Singapore through three legal pillars which I will outline.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, continually strengthening our legal framework in which we operate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our approach is to grow new areas to support emerging industries and evolving business models as well as to continue to build on our areas of strength.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, in the area of IP, which Mr Keith Chua spoke about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The value of an enterprise is increasingly in IP as well as in intangible assets (IA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But to realise this value, enterprises must be able to monetise both the IA and the IP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Only then will they be willing to invest in further innovation, which then further enhances and increases the value of their enterprise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore's IP regime and innovation environment are recognised internationally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We support enterprises at various stages of their IP journey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will provide enterprises with comprehensive IA and IP strategy support, including connecting with experts for a four-month mentorship.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Ms Sylvia Lim's query, for smaller enterprises and freelancers in the creative sectors, IPOS has simple info-packs as well as easy-to-understand videos that explain copyright and share best practices on using and protecting IP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, Ms Lim, I remember that when I introduced the Bill that you spoke about, we had introduced as well the learner aids as well as these videos.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, IPOS also works with agencies like the National Arts Council (NAC) and the National Library Board (NLB), as well as industry partners, like Copyright Licensing and Administration Society of Singapore (CLASS) and the Visual, Audio, Creative Content Professionals Association (VICPA), to provide additional support.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: IPOS is also working on a video podcast with NAC and NLB to engage creatives in the music industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will be launched during World IP Day on 26 April later this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: IPOS also actively supports partner events, such as the International Federation of Reproduction Rights Organisations (IFRRO) World Congress to discuss copyright-related issues and developments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, going down to the basic industry, at that level, as well as elevating ourselves to world global thought leadership in these areas are all part of the efforts to enhance awareness and education in this space.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we will, indeed, look out for more opportunities to reach our creators to raise their awareness in this very quickly evolving environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Minister of State Murali Pillai will speak about the development of technology and its impact on IP rights.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The second pillar I want to speak about is dispute resolution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: From time to time, we all know businesses may run into disputes with others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is really part and parcel of doing business.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But they have to be resolved in an open, transparent manner, as well as efficiently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Over the years, we have updated our regime and enhanced our services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We develop a full suite of options, whether it is in arbitration, mediation or litigation, or a combination of them, so that parties can choose, have the autonomy, depending on the nature of their needs as well as the particular circumstances of the transaction in question.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also give effect to party autonomy, be it choice of law or choice of forum, institution, modality of resolution, or the choice of counsel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If you take SICC, it is celebrating its 10th anniversary this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It has seen a steadily increasing caseload, including fresh filings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The caseload of SIAC, as well as SIMC, in both the arbitration and mediation spaces, have also seen a general upward trend.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many of these cases, in fact, have minimal connection to Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Mr Keith Chua's query, we will continue to strengthen our institutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, by embracing technology to provide value-added services to users.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIMC has a Mediation AI Assistant, and Maxwell Chambers offers cutting-edge drone camera and holographic displays which aid in the presentation of evidence, as well as in the course of resolving disputes at hearings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, by providing platforms to profile Singapore as a thought leader in this space.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members will know that we have many international conferences in Singapore, such as the Singapore Convention Week that started since 2019 in the starting days of the Singapore Convention on Mediation which we have continued since.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have the Singapore-China International Commercial Dispute Resolution Conference.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This takes place once a year – one year in China, and one year we hosted in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will host it in Singapore later this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These events, among others, not only provide a platform for leading experts to discuss latest developments, but they are also an opportunity for lawyers in Singapore to connect with the global community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is an integral part of a well-functioning and well-developed economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It provides practical and commercial options for companies as well as smaller businesses and entrepreneurs in financial distress, giving flexibility and realistic options to restructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Successful restructurings not only allow the debtor to carry on as a going concern, but generally result in better outcomes for employees, creditors and investors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry has enhanced this framework over the last decade and let me speak about three parts of this framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have grafted in features from leading, as well as tried-and-tested models, like, for example, chapter 11 of the US Bankruptcy Code, which we brought in about six to seven years ago.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have a differentiated discharge framework for bankrupts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a rehabilitative regime that seeks to encourage financial prudence without, at the same time, stifling entrepreneurship.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have arrived at a regime, which we believe, balances the interests of debtors and creditors, maintaining a healthy lending environment for sustained economic growth whilst, at the same time, supporting debtors across the spectrum: from individual entrepreneurs to larger corporates, both locally as well as foreign.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This has resulted in the growing use of Singapore's framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, the shipping firm, Pacific International Lines, and Vietnamese developer, No Va Land – a case heard in the SICC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Mr Zhulkarnain's and Mr Vikram Nair's queries, we are not resting on our laurels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are building on the experiences of these cases, as well as the experience of practitioners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are carefully looking at the next set of refinements, considering feedback and we will look at introducing further enhancements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These enhancements that we are thinking about will include the following.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, the Debt Repayment Scheme (DRS) for individuals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw is looking to, among other matters, prevent misuse of the DRS by debtors who are advised by businesses to borrow irresponsibly and then self-petition for bankruptcy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, in the area of corporate rescue tools, in particular, in judicial management.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also review our current Chapter 11 regime, to assess the need for changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, I move to the second pillar: expanding and growing our legal competency as well as capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Zhulkarnain said, for our law firms and our legal professionals to compete effectively, they must keep up with emerging trends and offer unique advantages and we agree with that.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To raise the quality and consistency of training, we implemented several changes in July 2024, pursuant to the Committee for the Professional Training of Lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The syllabus for the course leading up to Part B of the Bar Examinations was expanded to cover a wider range of topics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The practice training period was lengthened to one year, to allow trainees more time to gain exposure to contrasting practice areas and develop a strong all-rounded foundation as they start their practice career.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Ms Nadia Samdin’s point, we recognise that small firms may occasionally need support to cope with these changes and we appreciate very much Ms Samdin's continual advocacy for young lawyers in this space.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Singapore Institute of Legal Education and the Law Society have released guides to help trainees and supervising solicitors navigate these changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Ms Samdin knows, it has been less than a year since we have commenced on this path, so we will take on board the experiences of young lawyers at smaller firms in the space but for the moment, the guidelines cover areas such as honorarium and leave.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And the Law Society also published available training positions on their website, so that they become easier for trainees to find a training position in contrasting practice areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Law Society also offers career counselling, mentorship and guidance on practice training contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And the Law Society will implement other measures if necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Besides raising professional standards, we are also looking to shift mindsets and raise skillsets in our law firms and in our lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One area in which we seek to do this is in that of technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the legal sector, AI can potentially perform tasks at the level of junior associates, but at a fraction of the time and cost.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But instead of seeing this as a threat, let us also look at this as an opportunity for lawyers to go up the value chain, to focus on higher-value tasks looking at front-facing work, client-facing work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Globally, law firms in other jurisdictions, like the United States (US) and United Kingdom (UK), leading jurisdictions, for example: they are embracing and harnessing legaltech in support of their work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To compete with them, our lawyers must also keep that open mindset and embrace legaltech.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Generative AI (Gen AI) was also added in 2024 as a feature through Copilot for SG law firms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also made legaltech accessible to Singapore law practices, by providing subsidies to defray the cost.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also be piloting a change management initiative in the second half of this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have heard some feedback from law firms that they require more support to improve their tech processes, whilst at the same time managing and juggling their existing priorities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will therefore deploy legaltech consultants to the firms keen to join the pilot to diagnose their technology needs and recommend the appropriate tools for them in the context of their practice areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Another area which I wish to speak about is civil law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore is a common law jurisdiction, but many of our top trading partners come from civil law jurisdictions, such as China and Indonesia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, to position our lawyers better, we will be deepening civil law content in law school curriculum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also continue to run the China Ready Programme as well as the Singapore-Shanghai Lawyers Exchange Programme, which help to provide lawyers with a deeper and more embedded understanding of China’s business and legal environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And if there is demand for similar programmes in other markets and other jurisdictions, we will be happy to consider.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The areas of practice are quickly moving and the thought leadership around the study of law and more importantly, the practice and application of law to the industry is quickly evolving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To encourage this, we refreshed the Continuing Professional Development (CPD) system and will be increasing the CPD requirements in phases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Lawyers can use and tap into the SkillsFuture funding for many of the courses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Besides lawyers, allied legal professionals and in-house counsel are also a vital part of our legal sector, as Mr Patrick Tay spoke about it a short while ago.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Singapore Academy of Law is working with the Law Society as well as the Singapore Corporate Counsel Association and Temasek Polytechnic on a Skills Framework for Legal Services and training roadmap.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These will be first introduced for lawyers, followed by in-house counsel and then allied legal professionals over the next few years in phases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Temasek Polytechnic will also be introducing new courses in legal technology and legal project management for allied legal professionals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They have got feedback that these are areas that participants and students are keen on and so they will develop modules along these lines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a small city-state, we need to be plugged into the global economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But to do so, we must enhance our networks and collaborate with others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This really is a win-win situation for us if we can manage it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We help partners meet their goals from Singapore and in doing so, bring work here into the Singapore jurisdiction, which might otherwise not be present in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Over the years, we have strengthened our legal cooperation with key and emerging markets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To give Members some examples, last year, we signed four Memorandum of Understanding (MOUs) – two with Saudi Arabia, one with India and one with Kazakhstan – further expanding our global outreach into new markets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I have also made several trips in the course of last year to develop connections and help our law firms and lawyers build inroads into these markets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Zhulkarnain noted, we also increased our efforts to anchor in Singapore multilateral dispute resolution institutions, which administer disputes involving and including sovereign interests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This contributes to the international rule of law, as well as burnishes Singapore’s attractiveness as a premier dispute resolution hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also continue to welcome international law firms and foreign lawyers to anchor their presence here in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore has gradually liberalised the legal sector since the 1990s and this has benefited Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Over the years, we have introduced various schemes, to allow foreign law firms to collaborate with our local law firms and the schemes are attenuated to fit the level of collaboration that the foreign lawyers want with the local counterparts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These schemes have been successful, but we will continue to review them – to refine the framework where necessary, and also how we can rationalise and streamline them, with one aim being to reduce the regulatory burden on the law firms complying with these schemes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I should add that we will not change our posture of being open.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We remain open to foreign law firms and lawyers, while remaining committed to preserving the Singapore core in the legal profession.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chairman, the sum of our work contributes to the economy by facilitating businesses and attracting investments, allowing Singapore to thrive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Overall, we have been successful in playing this role.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And in 2023, Singapore was ranked second by the World Bank for net inflows of foreign direct investments (FDIs), behind only the US.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, by and large, these measures that I have spoken about, they have been successful in uplifting the Singapore business environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chairman, in the second part of my speech, I will focus on the domestic context.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In recent times, many countries have seen their social fabric under stress and divisions forming, as parts of society feel left out and trust in institutions diminishes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In Singapore, we are fortunate that we remain united; but we cannot for once take this for granted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our cohesive social fabric is underpinned by the rule of law and access to justice, and these are core pillars of our society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, we must continue to reinforce these fundamentals to maintain social trust and cohesion as well as uplift people’s lives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our laws form the bedrock of society – how it is ordered; how it functions; and how its members behave and interact in this society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In our community, when individuals or businesses face friction with each other, they have a range of options to resolve their disputes and differences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This involves going before an impartial adjudicator or working with a trusted mediator and through this process, parties present their perspectives and find resolution in their conflict.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A key part of this process is enforcement that some Members spoke about – that "last mile", where parties realise their rights, obtain redress and then move on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This has been a matter of focus for my Ministry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: When a party receives a judgment, this must be enforced effectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Otherwise, it is only really a paper judgment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have therefore been working to strengthen enforcement in two key areas: first in family justice; and second in civil judgments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where relations break down, we want to help to reduce the acrimony and allow parties to heal and to move on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A key improvement was the creation of the Maintenance Enforcement Process (MEP), as highlighted by Mr Zhulkarnain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Unfortunately, the reality is that there remains a fairly high incidence of non-compliance with maintenance orders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is also a significant number of repeat applications for enforcement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, under the MEP, Maintenance Enforcement Officers (MEOs) are empowered to obtain information about the parties’ financial circumstances and these findings will help the Courts make more effective maintenance enforcement orders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They can also facilitate settlements between the parties, which encourages more sustainable outcomes and judgments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A new unit of MEOs in MinLaw have started taking cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They will progressively expand their operations in phases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Mr Patrick Tay and Ms Jean See’s queries, MinLaw will also introduce reforms to make the enforcement of civil judgments more effective, simple and streamlined.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These reforms will be made available to our civil courts, which includes tribunals such as: the Employment Claims Tribunal, which Mr Tay spoke about; the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals; as well as the Small Claims Tribunal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They depart from the existing framework for enforcement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are currently studying them, evaluating them and consulting with interested parties, including Members of the Bar and the Judiciary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: More details will be released in due course as we complete this study.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This ensures they receive help and no one is left behind.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Mr Vikram Nair and Assoc Prof Razwana's queries, MinLaw has had a long history, being at the forefront of providing aid and assistance in the civil and criminal spheres including through programmes, such as the Legal Aid Bureau (LAB), for instance; and more recently, the Public Defender's Office (PDO).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Since 1958, LAB has provided the vulnerable with civil legal aid, including in matrimonial, monetary claims as well as probate matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Beyond taking on legal cases, LAB has strengthened connections in the community, for example, by organising networking sessions between family lawyers and social service professionals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw has been supporting the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS) as well, which is administered by Pro Bono SG, and progressed to directly fund them since 2015.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And from December 2022, PDO was operationalised to facilitate access to justice for more accused persons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Today, it has a team of 22 public defenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A part of these eligible applications is referred to CLAS, and between CLAS and PDO, they serve the section of the community who are most vulnerable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This partnership exemplifies the pro bono spirit among the legal fraternity – a partnership between the Government as well as Pro Bono SG, which is really ground-up, supported by many lawyers in the private sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This helps us to ensure that legal aid remains accessible not just across the criminal spectrum, which CLAS and PDO looks after, but also across the civil sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Last year, we updated the quantum of the per capita household income (PCHI) as well as the Annual Value (AV) for eligibility criteria to ensure that, in the light of increase in household income and property value in recent years, we will continue to serve the target audience and target persons who need assistance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We continually review these thresholds to ensure that they are kept in line.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Mr Sitoh Yih Pin's queries, the enhancements will be implemented shortly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Following the pilot, we will consider how to sustainably scale-up the process island-wide.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On mediation, as touched on by Assoc Prof Razwana, the Community Mediation Centre (CMC) continues to promote the benefits of mediation through channels like social media as well as everyday advertisements, such as those we see at the bus stops, for instance, to reach out to those who might need awareness brought to them about these schemes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To manage the anticipated increase in caseload, around 30 duty mediators have been identified to manage directed mediation cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will allow more convenience as well as improve accessibility.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I have spoken about our approach in growing the economy and maintaining trust and cohesion in society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are two very important outcomes of the work that we do at MinLaw.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore's success is underpinned by our strong legal system, based on the rule of law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That is something that is really non-negotiable for us in all the work that we do at MinLaw.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On this note, I would like to inform Members that we will be commemorating next year, the 200th anniversary of the establishment of Singapore's modern legal system via the Second Charter of Justice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It was in 1826 – next year will be 200 years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A series of events will take place to commemorate the occasion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: More details will be announced in due course.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I hope that Members will come and support these programmes and events next year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I would cover three broad areas: first, the prudent and imaginative use of state assets; second, safeguarding our society from concerns posed by emerging technologies; and third, access to justice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The Singapore Land Authority (SLA) ensures effective and imaginative use of land resources.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: To address Mr Zhulkarnain and Ms Nadia Samdin's queries, this is done by cultivating a good understanding of social and community needs through proactive engagement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: For example, SLA engages the National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre and community entities, such as New Hope, to understand their challenges in finding suitable spaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Through such engagements, SLA identified emerging demands, such as silver co-living and the need for community spaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Proposals with holistic programming and emphasis on inter-generational co-living that encourages independent senior living will be favourably considered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Second, SLA is activating state properties with potential to bring communities together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: One example is the transformation of 30 Maxwell Road into a wellness and fitness hub through the joint initiative with URA, Reinventing Spaces into Vibrant Places, as noted by Mr Keith Chua.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Another example is the transformation of the former Elections Department office at 11 Prinsep Street into a social impact hub named The Foundry, which started operations last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Further, SLA will restore and repurpose Block 1 East Coast Road (1ECR) for community and social uses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The renovated space will provide programmes and training to support youths as well as recreational activities for all ages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: SLA will continue collaborating with agencies to introduce more state properties for economic and social uses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: By launching more Price-Quality tenders, SLA will be able to better curate placemaking efforts to benefit the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Besides optimising the use of state assets, we are harnessing technology to digitalise transactions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Singapore's current conveyancing system is reliant on physical documents and processes, and requires significant manpower.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: SLA has therefore been developing the Digital Conveyancing Portal (DCP).

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: It is a fully integrated digital end-to-end conveyancing process for all types of property, from the stage of Option to Purchase (OTP) to legal completion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: It will also enable e-payments and digital documents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: When operationalised, the DCP will provide greater convenience to all parties, including buyers and sellers, law firms, real estate professionals, financial institutions and developers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are testing the system rigorously and seeking industry feedback, including on how the phases of the DCP should be prioritised and the continuing evolution of associated technology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Beta testing of the OTP process started in November 2024 with selected stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The DCP functions and types of transactions will be progressively expanded in subsequent phases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Even as technology becomes integral, we are aware that it also presents issues, particularly with copyright.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Our IP regime incentivises the creation of new works by rewarding creators with a set of rights over the use of their works, at the same time, allows reasonable access to these works by third parties, including other creators and innovators, who may build on them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In this way, we maximise creative and innovative output through a balanced approach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim and Ms Jean See asked about the balance in the context of AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: While the IP regime enables the use of copyright materials for digital innovation, we have built in conditions to protect legitimate interests of rights-holders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In particular, if copyright materials are used to train AI models, the materials must be lawfully accessed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: For example, for materials behind pay walls, through paid access.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Furthermore, rights-holders can use the copyright protection regime to take action against the generation or use of content substantially similar to their own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We recognise technologies, such as Gen AI, significantly impact many stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The Government remains committed to working with the creative community to address their concerns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: There is ongoing engagement with stakeholders, including those in the creative sector, such as writers, publishers, record labels and creative agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Some of the suggestions received include greater transparency in how copyright material is used for AI training and for rights-holders to have more control over use of their material.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: For example, we are exploring with MDDI and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), support for transparency measures and respect for copyright in our AI governance policies and tools, such as IMDA's upcoming safety guidelines for Gen AI model developers and app deployers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MinLaw and the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) will continue to work with stakeholders to maintain the right balance that will support creativity and innovation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We also focus on the impact of technology in the legal sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The need for guardrails is clear because: one, Gen AI may give inaccurate responses or hallucinate; two, security and privacy concerns – some Gen AI models may store user information and search history to train the model and this may then be reproduced for responses to other users; and three, ethical concerns with the rapid development of Gen AI by different programmers, it is critical that Gen AI tools are developed within a framework guided by principles, ethics and rules.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We have consulted stakeholders, such as the Singapore Courts, Law Society and IMDA, and will consult the industry in due course.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Another facet of digitalisation is the emerging threats to users and our community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Zhulkarnain and Ms Nadia Samdin asked about the Government's efforts to combat online harms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The Government has taken significant steps to address the prevalence of online harms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This includes, among others, enacting the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA) in 2014 and strengthening it in 2019, to provide victims with legal recourse for harassment, including online harassment; and enacting the Online Safety, Miscellaneous (Amendments) Act and the Online Criminal Harms Act to allow the Government to act against harmful content.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: However, online harms continue to be an area of concern for many – and hon Members said that in their speeches too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: A 2024 survey by MDDI found that two-thirds of respondents encountered harmful content on social media.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Online harms are an especially serious problem for the young and young women in particular.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In a 2023 study by SG Her Empowerment (SHE), more than half of the respondents between 15 and 24 years old reported having personally experienced online abuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This was more than in any other age group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Within this age group, young women were nearly twice as likely as men to be victims of sexual harassment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: And 40% of victims of online harassment reported suffering severe emotional and psychological distress, including depression and self-harm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MinLaw and MDDI have been studying the gaps that remain.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We have consulted extensively with community groups, such as those working with youths, and women and girls; experts; technology companies; and the Judiciary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The key gaps identified are the need for a simple and fast process to seek relief from online harms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The Court process can be daunting and difficult to navigate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Uncertainty over whether existing laws can be used to address new emerging harms and the lack of accountability as perpetrators are often anonymous.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: First, it will establish a new agency that will act quickly on complaints of online harms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MDDI will share more details about the agency as well as some of its broader efforts to deal with online harms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Second, it will set out Statutory Torts to clarify the types of online harms covered under the law, and the rights and duties of the various parties in the online ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: These Statutory Torts will provide a clear legal basis for victims to hold to account those responsible for the harm they suffer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We intend for the Statutory Torts to apply to a range of serious online harms, including online harassment, intimate image abuse and child abuse material.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Third, it will introduce new mechanisms to address the misuse of anonymity by perpetrators of online harms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As Ms Nadia Samdin and others have rightly observed – there must be adequate information in the first place, if the intent is to enhance accountability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Victims may apply to find out a perpetrator's user information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The victim may need to know, so as to consider legal proceedings, better protect himself or herself from the perpetrator.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The provision of such information will be subject to safeguards, to prevent abuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The information should not be used to carry out "counter-attacks".

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Stakeholders, such as the tech companies, have also expressed some reservations – mainly about how such measures will impact their business.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will work closely with them to mitigate their concerns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will announce more details in due course.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The Government is committed to ensuring that victims have accessible and effective remedies when they suffer online harms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked for figures relating to the Protection from Harassment Court (PHC).

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Previously, persons accused of such offences could only be released on bail while awaiting investigations or trial.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: They will be remanded if they are unable to find a bailor, even if they are offered bail.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: With this amendment, they may be released by putting up a bond by themselves in appropriate cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This reduces the disruptions to their lives and earning capacity, as mentioned by the hon Member.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The personal bond regime is new and in its infancy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will continue to keep our policies on remand and bail under review.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Lastly, I turn to our work on ensuring access to justice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Second Minister Edwin mentioned about the good work of the Public Defender's Office and the Legal Aid Bureau.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MinLaw is also working with various partners to increase access to justice, including through technology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Notably, we have collaborated with Pro Bono SG to develop LawGoWhere.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This year, a legal help finder will be integrated, to make it easier for users to seek legal information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Users may key in information such as their postal code and legal issue, and receive legal assistance options, such as their nearest legal clinics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Even as the use of technology increases, we are mindful of the digital divide, a point that Dr Tan Wu Meng made.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: On his query, measures have been taken to ensure that justice remains accessible to everyone, regardless of their level of familiarity with technology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: For example, individuals who have difficulties with Court e-services, like the Community Justice and Tribunals System, can contact the State Courts by calling their hotline.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: They may also visit the State Courts Business Centre to access digital terminals or approach the State Courts Service Hub if they require assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Before I conclude, Mr Chairman, I would like to thank hon Members for their comments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Ms Usha Chandradas spoke about possible areas for law reform.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Given the full slate of work outlined, some of these reviews will require more time for careful consideration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I understand from the Ministry of Social and Family Development that the same also applies to the 2000 Protection of Adults Convention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This was covered by the Ministry of Home Affairs in their COS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, in conclusion, Second Minister Edwin Tong spoke about the importance of the law and legal processes on achieving good outcomes for Singapore, underpinned by the rule of law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
